claims.text: The starting high-entropy alloy may have an FCC or BCC crystal structure.
High-entropy alloys contain multiple principal elements in equal or near-equal proportions.
The proposed intervention is addition of 1–2 at.% lanthanum.
Lanthanum is a large-atomic-radius or large-lattice-parameter element relative to the constituents of the host alloy.
Adding lanthanum to the high-entropy alloy will introduce lattice distortions.
Atomic-radius-driven lattice distortion increases phonon scattering in high-entropy materials.
Increased phonon scattering reduces the phonon mean free path.
Lattice distortion and the resulting phonon scattering reduce lattice or phonon thermal conductivity.
Adding 1–2 at.% lanthanum will reduce phonon thermal conductivity by 10–20% relative to the untreated alloy.
The untreated comparator has the same composition as the treated alloy but contains no added lanthanum.
The treated and untreated alloys should have the same processing history.
The predicted conductivity reduction will hold from 300 to 1000 K.
The predicted conductivity reduction applies to polycrystalline alloys with grain sizes greater than 1 micrometre.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity reduction may depend on the host-alloy composition and processing history.
Lanthanum addition may affect strength or corrosion resistance.
The hypothesis is defined as falsified if conductivity is reduced by less than 5% or if no lattice distortion is detected.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as having the same composition as the lanthanum-doped alloy while simultaneously containing no added lanthanum. It can only be otherwise compositionally comparable, not literally the same composition.

The predicted reduction is 10–20%, but the falsification threshold is below 5%; a measured reduction from 5% to under 10% would contradict the stated prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
